title: Representations and information paths
goals: Trace information through a system without confusing information with a physical action
Explain which details a representation preserves or discards
Locate the earliest stage at which an incorrect result could have arisen

prerequisite.prompt: In last week's bus case, the forecast number and the display colour came from different decisions. Which decision produced each output?
prerequisite.answer: The fitted model produced the delay estimate; the written greater-than-10 rule selected the colour. A caretaker or driver decision is a separate action.

vocabulary: A way of recording information so that it can be stored, communicated or processed
Information supplied to a particular process
An operation that changes, selects or interprets information
The result produced by a process
Details that cannot be recovered from the retained representation

lesson.title: A display does not do every part of a task

blocks.text: A library kiosk asks Sam for a genre. Sam selects mystery. The kiosk compares that preference with catalogue tags and displays three book titles. Sam says the kiosk has read three books aloud. That conclusion adds an action that the description never supplied: displaying a title is different from producing spoken audio.

An information path names what enters each stage, what happens there and what leaves it. Treat input and output as roles relative to a stage. A list of titles is the output of the search, but it could become the input to a separate text-to-speech stage. A component can therefore receive the output of another component without doing the same job.

The kiosk's genre-matching operation can be implemented with a written rule. Nothing in this description establishes that a model was trained. This connects to Week 1: tracing information tells us what a process needs to do, while mechanism evidence tells us how it does it.

blocks.title: Two possible library information paths
rows: Genre request mystery and catalogue tags
Three titles from the first stage
A separate speech system if available
Spoken titles rather than whole books
A selected title and an available copy
A person completes the borrowing process
A recorded loan and a borrowed copy
blocks.caption: The first row is the kiosk as described. The later rows require additional components and actions. Arrows show information dependencies; they do not establish that every stage has actually run.

blocks.text: Notice the difference between a title, a description and an entire book. All three can be text, but they represent different amounts of information. Even a speech stage receiving three titles can speak only those supplied titles; it has not thereby read the full books. Always identify the content of an input, not just its data type.

A recommendation is also different from a loan. Selecting a title does not reserve a copy unless an authorised reservation step exists. Keeping these distinctions clear prevents us from crediting a system with actions it did not take.

Consider two catalogue records. Book A has 90 pages and is about a child solving a seaside mystery. Book B has 90 pages and is about a lost spaceship. If we keep only page count, both become the number 90. The number is useful for a length limit, but it cannot tell us which story is a mystery. Information that was never retained cannot be recovered just by calculating harder.

rows: Does it match a mystery request?
Will this particular reader enjoy it?
What does the description say happens?
What exact sentence occurs on page 42?

blocks.text: The phrase cannot settle alone matters. A genre tag might be inaccurate, and a reader might enjoy an unfamiliar genre. A representation is useful only in relation to a question and its limits. More detail is not automatically better: unnecessary personal information can add risk without helping the task.

A greenhouse records morning temperatures of 18, 22 and 26 degrees C, then retains only the largest value, 26. Can the stored value prove that the temperature rose steadily? No. The sequence 22, 18, 26 has the same largest value but includes a decrease. These two sequences form a counterexample to the claim that the largest value determines the order.

To solve this, first state exactly what was kept: one maximum. Then ask what the claim requires: the order of several readings. Finally construct two possible originals that share the retained value but give different answers to the claim. If both originals fit the record, the record alone cannot decide between them.

blocks.label: A record keeps only a visitor count of 3. Give two different arrival schedules consistent with it and name one fact the count cannot reveal

blocks.text: The kiosk is asked for mystery books under 100 pages but displays a 140-page mystery. Before changing everything, inspect the intermediate records. Was the maximum entered as 100? Did the catalogue say 140? Did filtering preserve the wrong record? Did the display show a title different from the filtered result? The first mismatch between the intended and actual path helps locate the problem.

A correct-looking final screen can hide an earlier error. A calculator can correctly multiply a number that was transcribed incorrectly, and a warning rule can correctly use an incorrect forecast. Write down intermediate values so you can test each connection.

blocks.label: Explain why a system that displays a book title has not necessarily spoken, reserved or read the book

workbook.title: Trace a request
workbook.prompt: The kiosk receives genre=science and maximum pages=120. The catalogue contains A science 80 pages, B science 150 pages and C mystery 90 pages. It keeps records with the requested genre and no more than 120 pages. Draw the input, process and output, naming the surviving record.
workbook.answer: Input includes both request fields and all three catalogue records. The process checks science AND pages<=120. Output contains A only; B fails the length condition and C fails the genre condition. Listing A does not establish that a copy was reserved.

workbook.title: Finish the visitor example
workbook.prompt: A record stores only total visitors=3. Give two different arrival schedules that produce this total. Can the total tell us the busiest hour? Explain.
workbook.answer: Examples: three visitors at 09:00, or one each at 09:00, 10:00 and 11:00. Both total 3, but their busiest-hour patterns differ. The total lacks arrival-time information, so the busiest hour cannot be recovered from it alone.

workbook.title: Choose a sufficient representation
workbook.prompt: For each task, choose the information needed: decide whether a book is under 120 pages; quote its first sentence exactly; decide whether a copy is available now. Explain why a genre tag alone is insufficient for all three.
workbook.answer: Use the page count for the length condition, the actual first sentence from the correct edition for an exact quote, and a current copy-availability record for availability. Genre supplies none of those facts. Even suitable records must be checked for the correct edition or time.

workbook.title: Investigate a new loss of information
workbook.prompt: A classroom device receives four scores and stores only their total, 20. A student claims that every score must be 5. Give two different lists of four nonnegative whole-number scores with total 20. Explain precisely what the stored total establishes and what it does not.
workbook.answer: For example [5,5,5,5] and [2,4,6,8] both total 20. The stored total establishes the sum under the stated recording process, but not the individual scores or their equality. A list with fewer than four entries or a different total is not a valid counterexample.

workbook.title: Diagnose before repairing
workbook.prompt: A voice calculator receives a spoken request for 16 divided by 4. Its transcript says 60 divided by 4 and its calculator returns 15. Identify the first incorrect stage, show the intended result and propose a check before calculation.
workbook.answer: Transcription first changes 16 to 60. The calculator correctly computes the wrong supplied expression. The intended result is 4. Display or confirm the interpreted numbers before calculating, rather than changing the arithmetic code to force the expected answer.

teacher.background: Teach input and output as relative to a stage. Avoid claiming that representations are inherently truthful or complete. This lesson introduces information loss through counterexamples, without requiring formal information theory. The two-originals method is the important reasoning move: if two source records map to one stored result but imply different answers, the stored result cannot decide that question alone.
materials: Catalogue records A science 80, B science 150 and C mystery 90 written on cards
The information-path diagram and blank arrow diagrams
Paper for two four-number lists; no devices or accounts are needed
sessions: Retrieve the bus stages from Week 1. Ask which result becomes a later input.
Read the kiosk case and trace the first diagram row. Cover later rows, then reveal them as additional operations rather than assumed capabilities.
Use the two 90-page book descriptions. Ask which question survives when only 90 is kept. Model one counterexample.
Pairs complete W1 and the visitor example. Require exact input fields and outputs.
Ask whether a largest temperature proves a rising sequence. Have two students construct alternative sequences.
Complete W2 and W3. Separate current records, exact source text and summary tags.
Collect W4 independently. Give no example list until the attempt is saved.
Use W5 to connect information loss with stage diagnosis. Review the exit explanation and preview measurement.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Visitor schedules can be three at 09:00 or one each at 09:00, 10:00 and 11:00. The total does not reveal timing or busiest hour. Displaying a book title produces text on a screen; speaking needs audio generation, reserving needs an authorised availability update and reading the whole book needs its full content.
misconceptions: Every output is the final action
Trace an output entering the next stage. Ask whether the borrowing or speech stage exists and has run.
More calculation can recover discarded details
Ask students to distinguish two original records with the same retained value. No deterministic calculation of that value alone can know which original occurred.
A data type tells us what the data means
Compare a title, a summary and a full chapter. All can be text while supporting different questions.
teacher.assessment: W4 is secure when both lists contain four nonnegative whole numbers, both sum to 20, at least one is not all fives, and the explanation distinguishes sum from individual values. If the learner offers only one list, request another record consistent with the same total. Use a different total for the uncoached retry.
teacher.support: Provide four empty boxes and counters for learners who need arithmetic support. Let them explain information loss orally. Extension: ask which extra field, such as minimum score, would rule out one of their lists and whether it would uniquely determine the original list.
teacher.next: Week 3 examines how physical signals become measurements, including the units and conditions needed to interpret recorded values.
